title: Stay Awake
sum: Jesus leaves the Temple for the last time. When a disciple admires its huge stones, he says that not one will be left on another. On the Mount of Olives, facing the Temple, his first four disciples ask him privately when this will happen and what sign will come first. His answer is Mark's longest speech.

He warns them not to be led astray by claimants and not to panic at wars and earthquakes, which are only the start of the labor pains. They will be put on trial before councils, governors and kings; families will betray them; the good news must first reach all the nations. When they see "the abomination of desolation" standing where he must not stand, those in Judea must run. After that suffering the sky will go dark, and the Son of Man will come in clouds and gather his chosen. The fig tree teaches that the end is near, yet no one, not even the Son, knows the day. So: stay awake.

Matthew 24 is the fuller form of this speech, and its chapter page has the deep dives on the Jewish War, the four ways of reading the speech, and its parallels in Revelation. This page focuses on what Mark adds, on what chapter 13 tells us about when Mark was written, and on the speech's last word, "stay awake."
readings: Read as history

Jesus' prophecy that the Temple would fall came true in AD 70. Historians who doubt that Jesus could foresee it date Mark after 70, or just before, when the war had begun; others argue that a prophet who watched Rome's power and the Temple's leaders could well have warned of the city's fall, as Jeremiah and Micah had. The persecutions of 13:9–13 match what Acts, Paul's letters and Tacitus say happened to Jesus' followers.
Read as a call to watchfulness

Whatever one decides about its timetable, the speech is mostly commands: watch out, do not be fooled, do not panic, hold out, run when it is time, stay awake. It begins with "Be on your guard" (13:5) and ends with "stay awake!" (13:37). Its aim is to keep the disciples faithful through confusion, not to satisfy curiosity about dates.
Read with the rest of Mark

The speech stands between Jesus' judgment on the Temple (11:12–12:44) and his passion (14–15). Its warnings come true almost at once in miniature: the disciples are "handed over" in fear, they fall asleep, the rooster crows, the hour comes at evening, midnight, cockcrow and dawn, and the sky goes dark at noon.

views.H: The Temple Herod rebuilt was one of the wonders of the Roman world; it was burned in August AD 70 and its buildings torn down. Between Jesus' death and that year, Judea saw would-be prophets and messiahs, famines (Acts 11:28), earthquakes, the emperor Gaius's attempt to set up his statue in the Temple (AD 40), and from 66 the Jewish revolt. Christians were tried before Jewish and Roman courts (Acts; 2 Corinthians 11:24–26), and in Rome in AD 64 Nero had many burned and torn by dogs (Tacitus). A tradition reported by Eusebius says the Jerusalem church fled to Pella before the siege.
views.C: Chapter 13 is central to dating Mark (see the deep dive). Most critical scholars place Mark between 65 and 75, in Rome or Syria, with chapter 13 written in the shadow of the Jewish War. Gerd Theissen argued that an earlier written warning from the Caligula crisis of AD 40 lies behind 13:14–20. Some scholars think the early church shaped Jesus' sayings into a short apocalypse; others hold that the core goes back to Jesus. Matthew and Luke both rework Mark 13, Luke making the siege of Jerusalem explicit (Luke 21:20).
views.L: The speech is framed by commands to "watch out" (13:5, 9, 23, 33) and to "stay awake" (13:34–37). It falls into a warning against false alarms (13:5–13), the great distress in Judea (13:14–23), the coming of the Son of Man (13:24–27), and two short parables about knowing and not knowing (13:28–37). Its last words reach past the four listeners to every reader (13:37), and the passion story that follows tests them at once.
views.J: The speech belongs to Jewish apocalyptic writing, like Daniel, 1 Enoch and 4 Ezra: birth pains before the new age, a time of distress like none before (Daniel 12:1), the desecration of the sanctuary (Daniel 9:27), the darkening of the sky (Isaiah 13:10), the gathering of scattered Israel (Deuteronomy 30:4). Jewish readers also mourned the Temple's fall, remembered every year on the ninth of Av. Readers should not turn a prophecy spoken by a Jew, in grief, about his own people's sanctuary into a gloating over Israel's ruin.
views.T: The church fathers read the chapter both of the fall of Jerusalem and of the end of the world: Eusebius saw its fulfillment in Josephus's account of the war, while Hippolytus and others looked for a future Antichrist in the abomination. "Nor the Son" (13:32) became a key text in the debates with the Arians in the 300s. The call to "stay awake" shaped the church's Advent season and its vigils of prayer through the night.

deep.h: When was Mark written? The evidence of chapter 13
deep.b:
Mark gives no date, and the early church remembered two answers. Irenaeus (about 180) says Mark wrote down Peter's preaching after the "departure" of Peter and Paul, probably meaning their deaths in the 60s. Clement of Alexandria (as Eusebius reports) says Mark wrote while Peter was still preaching in Rome. Most modern scholars date Mark between 65 and 75, and chapter 13 is the main reason.

  • Before AD 70. Martin Hengel and others argue that Mark wrote during the war, about 68–69. The speech warns of a coming disaster but gives none of the details a writer after 70 would add: no fire in the Temple (Luke 19:43–44 and Matthew 22:7 are more vivid), no siege of the city in Mark, and a flight "to the mountains" that does not match the tradition of a flight to Pella in the Jordan valley.
  • An older source, a later Gospel. Gerd Theissen traces the warning behind 13:14–20 to the crisis of AD 40, when the emperor Gaius ordered his statue set up in the Temple: a man ("he") standing where he must not. But he dates the Gospel itself shortly after 70; only the leaflet it used is earlier.
  • Just after AD 70. Joel Marcus and others argue that Mark wrote soon after the Temple fell. "Not one stone left on a stone" matches what happened; the Zealot leaders who occupied the Temple in 67–68, or Titus entering the holy place, fit "standing where he must not"; and the urgent "let the reader understand" suggests events the readers had just lived through.
  • Earlier. A few scholars date Mark to the 40s or 50s, holding that Jesus' prophecy was simply that and tells us nothing about when Mark wrote.

For readers who accept that Jesus could foretell the future, the prophecy does not fix the date. For those who do not, it points to the years around 70. Either way, Mark wrote for Christians who had faced or would soon face trials and the shock of the war, which is why the speech says so much about holding out and so little about dates.

Matthew follows Mark 13 closely but enlarges it. The chapter page for Matthew 24 has the deep dives on the Jewish War, the four ways of reading the speech (preterist, futurist, the near and far view, and the critical view), Matthew, Mark and Luke side by side, and the parallels in Revelation. What is distinctive in Mark:

  • The listeners are named: Peter, James, John and Andrew (13:3).
  • The disciples ask only about the Temple; Matthew adds "your coming and the completion of the age" (Matthew 24:3).
  • The warning of trials (13:9–13) stands in the speech; Matthew moved most of it to the mission speech in Matthew 10:17–22.
  • "First the good news must be proclaimed to all the nations" (13:10).
  • "Standing where he must not stand," with a masculine "he," and no mention of Daniel; the reader's aside then addresses Mark's own reader (13:14).
  • No "or on a Sabbath" (13:18; compare Matthew 24:20).
  • No "immediately" before the darkening of the sun (13:24).
  • "From the farthest edge of the earth to the farthest edge of the sky" (13:27).
  • "Nor the Son" is secure in Mark's manuscripts (13:32).
  • Mark ends with the brief parable of the doorkeeper and the four night watches (13:33–37); Matthew follows with Noah, the two slaves, the ten young women, the talents, and the sheep and goats.

deep.title: Claude's theory: a briefing for four, failed by three
deep.b: Mark alone says that chapter 13 was spoken privately to four men: Peter, James, John and Andrew (13:3). It ends with "stay awake" three times and the warning that the master may come "late in the evening, at midnight, at rooster crow, or at dawn" and find them sleeping (13:35–36). Two nights later Jesus takes three of the same four into Gethsemane, tells them "stay awake," and finds them sleeping three times (14:33–41); the rooster crows at Peter's denial; Jesus is handed over at dawn. I suggest that Mark has shaped the speech as a private briefing for exactly these men so that its first test falls on them, and that the missing Andrew sharpens the point: the three who saw Jesus' glory on the mountain (9:2) are the ones who fail. The link between 13:33–37 and the passion night is widely noted (R. H. Lightfoot, Joel Marcus and others); the role of the four named listeners, and of Andrew's absence, is my own suggestion and may read too much into a list of names.

echoes: Daniel 2:28; Daniel 7:13–14; Daniel 9:27; Daniel 11:31; Daniel 12:1; Daniel 12:11; Isaiah 13:10; Isaiah 34:4; Deuteronomy 30:4; Zechariah 2:6; Micah 7:6; Matthew 24:1–51; Matthew 10:17–22; Luke 21:5–36; Luke 12:35–40; 2 Thessalonians 2:1–12; Revelation 6:12–17

settings.to: one of his disciples, as they walk out of the Temple courts
settings.when: in Passover week, as Jesus leaves the Temple for the last time after his debates with its leaders (11:27–12:44). Matthew 24:1–2 has the disciples as a group point out the buildings; Luke 21:5–6 has "some" speaking about the Temple, with no change of place
settings.why: to answer admiration of the building with a warning: the house whose leaders he has judged (11:15–17; 12:1–12) will be torn down, and the disciples must not put their hope in its stones
settings.readers: Mark's readers, reading just before or just after AD 70, knew that the Temple was falling or had fallen; the scene told them that Jesus had foreseen it, and that their faith did not depend on it.

settings.what: The speech on the Mount of Olives
settings.to: Peter, James, John and Andrew, privately, sitting on the Mount of Olives across from the Temple
settings.when: apparently the same day, two days before Passover (14:1), though Mark's count of days is debated. Matthew 24:3 also sets the speech on the Mount of Olives, but to "the disciples" as a group; Luke 21:5–7 seems to keep Jesus in the Temple, speaking to a wider circle
settings.why: to prepare his closest followers for what would follow his death: false messiahs and alarms, trials and betrayals, the ruin of Jerusalem, and the coming of the Son of Man; to keep them from being deceived or frightened, and to make them watchful and faithful rather than date-setters
settings.readers: Mark's church heard the speech as addressed to them ("what I tell you, I tell everyone," 13:37; "the one who reads this," 13:14): believers who had faced or feared trial and betrayal, and who were trying to make sense of the Jewish War.
views: Christians in Rome after Nero's persecution of AD 64, hearing news of the war in Judea and claims that the end had come (Hengel and the traditional view).
Believers shaken by the Temple's fall, needing to hear that Jesus foretold it and that the Son of Man's coming was still to be awaited (Marcus and many others).
Many futurist readers hold that the speech, while spoken to the disciples, describes events that are still to come for the church.

settings.to: the four disciples
settings.when: within the speech on the Mount of Olives
settings.why: to tell them in advance that they will be handed over, as he will be, so that trials will not shake them, and to promise the Holy Spirit's help when they must speak
settings.readers: For Mark's readers, councils, floggings, governors, and family members informing on each other (as Tacitus reports of AD 64) were their own experience; "whoever holds out to the end" was the word they needed.

settings.to: the four disciples, about "those who are in Judea"
settings.when: within the speech
settings.why: to give a clear signal for flight when the sanctuary is defiled, and to warn against false messiahs and wonder-workers in the crisis
settings.readers: Mark breaks in to tell his reader to think about what it means (13:14): his first readers were meant to recognize a sign in their own time, perhaps the Caligula crisis, the Zealots in the Temple, or Titus's army.

settings.what: The parable of the fig tree
settings.to: the four disciples
settings.when: within the speech
settings.why: to teach that the signs he has described, when they come, mean that "it" is near, as new fig leaves mean summer
settings.readers: Mark's readers had just heard of a fig tree in leaf without fruit, cursed beside the Temple (11:12–21); the second fig tree turns the image to hope.

settings.to: the four disciples, and through them "everyone"
settings.when: the last words of the speech, and of Jesus' public teaching in Mark
settings.why: to tell them that since the day is unknown, even to the Son, the only right response is to work and keep watch, like slaves left in charge of a house and a doorkeeper told to stay awake
settings.readers: The parable reached every reader of Mark directly (13:37). Matthew and Luke have longer parables of absent masters; Mark's short form is aimed at the night watches the disciples were about to fail.

traditions.q: Jesus says of the day and hour that "the Son does not know. Only the Father knows" (13:32). How can the Son not know, and what does it say about who he is?
views: Christ is one person, fully God and fully man, and Orthodox writers are divided on how he could not know. Athanasius, against the Arians who used the verse to deny the Son's full divinity, says he did not know "as a man," in the human nature he truly took on, and for our sake. After the Agnoetae controversy of the 500s, John of Damascus and later Orthodox writers deny any real ignorance in Christ's human soul: he spoke of not knowing "by economy," taking on our condition and keeping the day hidden, a reading close to the Catholic one.

By its union with the divine Word, Christ's human knowledge had the fullness of understanding of the eternal plans he came to reveal; what he said he did not know in this area, he elsewhere showed he was not sent to reveal (Catechism 474, citing this verse and Acts 1:7).

Calvin held that Christ, in his human nature, truly did not know the day, and that this is no more against his divinity than his real hunger, fear and grief; as man he grew in wisdom (Luke 2:52) and was subject to the limits of a human mind.

Divided. Many Anglicans follow the older answer of the fathers, but the "kenotic" view was argued most fully by Charles Gore (1891, 1895): in becoming man the Son freely limited himself, emptying himself (Philippians 2:7), so that in his earthly life he truly did not know the day. The Lutheran theologian Gottfried Thomasius had made a similar case in the 1850s. The view is the main Protestant alternative to Calvin's, and its critics say it compromises the Son's unchanging divinity.
The verse shows that the Son is not equal to the Father: if they were one God, the Son would know what the Father knows. Jesus is God's firstborn Son, a mighty spirit being, but not Almighty God.

title: Anointed, Handed Over, Denied
sum: Two days before Passover the chief priests look for a way to kill Jesus quietly. At Bethany a woman breaks a jar of costly nard and pours it on his head; when others scold her, Jesus says she has anointed his body for burial and will be remembered wherever the good news is told. Judas goes to the priests to hand him over.

At the Passover meal Jesus says that one who eats with him will hand him over. He takes bread and a cup: "This is my body," "This is my blood of the covenant. It is being poured out for many." On the Mount of Olives he foretells that all will be tripped up and that Peter will deny him three times before the rooster crows twice. In Gethsemane he prays, "Abba, Father ... not what I want, but what you want," while his friends sleep. Judas arrives with a crowd and a kiss; all the disciples run, and a young man flees naked.

Before the high priest, false witnesses cannot agree. Asked whether he is the Messiah, Jesus answers "I am" and speaks of the Son of Man at God's right hand. The council condemns him for blasphemy and mocks him as a prophet, while in the courtyard below Peter denies him three times, the rooster crows a second time, and Peter bursts into tears.
readings: Read as history

Most historians agree that Jesus shared a last meal with his followers, was betrayed by one of them, was arrested at night outside the city, and was questioned by the high priest's circle before being handed to Pilate. They debate the date of the meal, the nature of the night hearing, and how much any witness could know of Gethsemane. Mark's account is probably the earliest written; Matthew and Luke follow it closely.
Read as Mark's story

Mark builds the chapter with two "sandwiches": the plot and Judas around the anointing (14:1–11), and Peter's denial around the trial (14:54–72). Each holds two kinds of disciple side by side: the woman who gives everything and the disciple who sells his master; the teacher who confesses under oath and the follower who denies with an oath. The word "all" runs through the night: all drink, all promise, all flee.
Read in the church's worship

The church relives this chapter in Holy Week. The words over the bread and cup are said at every celebration of the Eucharist or Lord's Supper; Holy Thursday or Maundy Thursday keeps the night of the Supper and the watch in Gethsemane; and Jesus' prayer, "not what I want, but what you want," has become the model of Christian prayer in anguish.

views.H: Passover in Jerusalem brought huge crowds and extra Roman troops; the high priest Caiaphas (Mark does not name him) held office from about AD 18 to 36 by working with Rome. A night arrest on the Mount of Olives avoided the crowds. Gethsemane, "oil press," was an olive grove across the Kidron. The details of the meal, the upper room and the reclining guests fit a Passover in Jerusalem; whether the meal was the Passover itself is debated (see 14:12 and the deep dive at Matthew 26).
views.C: Mark is probably the source for Matthew 26 and Luke 22. Matthew adds Judas's question and the thirty coins, "eat" and "so that sins can be forgiven"; Luke adds a second cup and "do this in remembrance of me." John tells the anointing differently (John 12:1–8), puts Jesus' death on the day the lambs were killed, and has no words over bread and cup at the supper. Mark alone has the man with the jar, "Abba," the young man who fled, the two cockcrows and Jesus' plain "I am."
views.L: Mark's chapter is a study of discipleship under pressure. The unnamed woman acts while the named disciples fail. Peter, James and John, who heard "stay awake" in chapter 13, sleep. The young man who flees naked is the last picture of following in Mark until the young man in white at the tomb (16:5). Jesus' honest "I am" before the high priest is set against Peter's three lies in the courtyard, and the guards' taunt "Be a prophet!" is answered by the rooster.
views.J: Jesus keeps Passover as a Jew among Jews, says the blessing over bread and wine, sings the Hallel, and prays to God as Father in Aramaic. The opposition comes from the chief priests and their circle, a small ruling elite in a tense political setting; the people, Mark says, were the reason they feared to act openly (14:2). Jewish scholars such as Geza Vermes, Paula Fredriksen and Amy-Jill Levine stress that the night hearing does not represent "the Jews," and that Mark's account was later used against Jewish communities in ways Mark never intended.
views.T: The church fathers saw in the anointing a sign of Christ's kingship and burial; in the Supper the institution of the Eucharist; in Gethsemane proof that Christ had a human will that freely yielded to the Father (Maximus the Confessor; the Third Council of Constantinople, 681). Peter's tears became the model of repentance, and the Orthodox call Holy Thursday the day of "the betrayal."

deep.b:
Matthew 26 follows Mark 14 scene by scene, and its chapter page has the deep dives on the Last Supper in Matthew, Mark, Luke and Paul; on whether the meal was a Passover; and on the trial before the Sanhedrin, with the Where Christians differ cards on Christ's presence in the bread and wine and on giving the cup to all. What only Mark has:

  • The woman's oil was "real nard," worth "over three hundred denarii," and she broke the jar (14:3–5).
  • The disciples will meet "a man carrying a clay jar of water" (14:13).
  • Jesus' prayer begins "Abba" (14:36), and he calls Peter "Simon" (14:37).
  • A young man flees naked (14:51–52).
  • The false witnesses "did not match" (14:56, 59), and the temple saying has "made by human hands" and "no hands made" (14:58).
  • Jesus answers the high priest with a plain "I am" (14:62).
  • The rooster crows twice (14:30, 68, 72).

deep.h: The young man who fled, and the Secret Gospel of Mark
deep.b:
The scene. Only Mark tells of a young man who followed Jesus wearing a linen cloth and fled naked when they grabbed him (14:51–52). The views on who he was are in the note at 14:51.

The "Secret Gospel" (a work in no church's Bible). In 1958 the American scholar Morton Smith, cataloguing books at the Greek Orthodox monastery of Mar Saba near Jerusalem, reported finding a handwritten Greek copy of a letter at the back of a printed book (a 1646 edition of the letters of Ignatius). The letter claims to be from Clement of Alexandria (about AD 200) to a certain Theodore. It says that Mark, after writing his Gospel in Rome, wrote in Alexandria a "more spiritual" version for those being initiated, and it quotes two passages. The first, placed after Mark 10:34, tells how Jesus raised a rich young man from a tomb in Bethany; six days later the young man came to Jesus at night "wearing a linen cloth over his naked body" and was taught "the mystery of the kingdom of God." The second, after 10:46, says that the sister of the young man whom Jesus loved, his mother and Salome were in Jericho and Jesus did not receive them. Smith published the letter in 1973.

Why it is not Scripture. No church has ever counted it as Scripture, and no ancient writer other than this letter mentions it. Even on its own account it was a later, expanded edition of Mark, not the original. The manuscript itself has never been examined by scientists. Several scholars saw it at Mar Saba in 1976; in 1977 the Patriarchate's librarian removed the pages from the book and had them photographed, in colour, and their present location is unknown. The pages are now lost; Smith's black-and-white photographs and the colour photographs of 1977 survive.

Reliability (a labeled analysis). Scholars are sharply divided. Against authenticity: Stephen Carlson (2005) and Peter Jeffery (2007) argue that Smith forged the letter, pointing to features of the handwriting, to themes that match Smith's own interests, and to anachronisms they find in its picture of ritual. For authenticity: Scott Brown (2005) and others argue that the letter's language and ideas fit Clement and Alexandria, that Smith could not have produced such a convincing imitation, and that the charges rest on misreadings. Handwriting experts consulted since 2009 have disagreed. A cautious summary: the letter may be an ancient text (whether by Clement or not), or a modern forgery; in either case it tells us about the later reception of Mark in Alexandria, or about the twentieth century, not about Jesus.

How to read it. As evidence in a debate, not as a source for the Gospel. Its young man in a linen cloth shows how readers noticed the strange figure of Mark 14:51–52 and tried to explain him. The Plain of Mark is translated from the Greek manuscripts and is untouched by it.

echoes: Exodus 12:1–27; Exodus 24:8; Deuteronomy 15:11; Deuteronomy 19:15; Psalm 41:9; Psalms 42–43; Psalm 110:1; Psalms 113–118; Isaiah 50:6; Isaiah 53:12; Jeremiah 31:31; Zechariah 9:11; Zechariah 13:7; Daniel 7:13; Amos 2:16; Matthew 26:1–75; Luke 22:1–71; John 12:1–8; John 13:1–30; John 18:1–27; 1 Corinthians 11:23–26

settings.by: the chief priests and the scribes
settings.to: one another
settings.when: two days before Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread
settings.why: to remove Jesus without starting a riot among the pilgrims who admired him
settings.readers: Mark's readers learned that Jesus' death was planned by a ruling group that feared the crowds, not by the people.

settings.what: Jesus defends the woman who anointed him
settings.to: the guests who scolded her, in the house of Simon in Bethany
settings.when: at a meal two days before Passover. Matthew 26:6–13 follows Mark; John 12:1–8 sets the anointing six days before Passover and names Mary of Bethany, and Luke 7:36–50 tells of a different anointing, in Galilee
settings.why: to stop their scolding, to show that her gift was right at this unrepeatable moment, to give it the meaning of an anointing for burial, and to promise that she would be remembered
settings.readers: For a church that told the good news "in the whole world," the promise was being kept as they read; and they were reminded that love poured out for Jesus is never wasted.

settings.to: two of his disciples
settings.when: on the day the Passover lambs were sacrificed
settings.why: to arrange a place for the meal, quietly and with a sign only the two would recognize
settings.readers: Mark's readers saw Jesus in command of events, as in the finding of the colt (11:1–6).

settings.to: the Twelve, reclining at the Passover meal
settings.when: during the meal
settings.why: to let them know that he goes to his death knowingly and as Scripture foretold, and to warn the betrayer, who is still among them
settings.readers: For a church that knew betrayal by its own members (13:12), the scene showed that even Jesus was betrayed by a friend at his table.

settings.what: The words over the bread and the cup
settings.to: the Twelve, at the Passover meal
settings.when: as they ate, on the night he was handed over
settings.why: to give his coming death its meaning: his body given, his blood poured out for many, a covenant sealed as at Sinai, and a promise of the feast in God's kingdom
settings.readers: Mark's church repeated these words at its own meal; reading them in the story of that night tied their worship to Jesus' death and hope.

settings.what: Jesus foretells the scattering and Peter's denial
settings.to: the Twelve, on the way to the Mount of Olives
settings.when: after the meal
settings.why: to warn them that they would fail, to show that even this was foreseen in Scripture (Zechariah 13:7), and to promise that he would regather them in Galilee
settings.readers: Readers who had themselves failed under pressure heard that Jesus knew his followers would fail and had promised to meet them again.

settings.to: his Father ("Abba"), with Peter, James and John nearby
settings.when: at night in the olive grove, after the supper
settings.why: to bring his dread before God, to ask to be spared, and to yield his will to the Father's; and to teach the three to stay awake and pray so as not to fall in testing
settings.readers: Mark's readers, praying under threat, had a model of honest prayer and surrender, and a warning in the sleeping disciples.

settings.to: the armed crowd sent by the chief priests, scribes and elders
settings.when: at his arrest in Gethsemane
settings.why: to expose the stealth of an arrest by night when he had taught openly every day, and to say that the Scriptures were being fulfilled
settings.readers: The scene told readers that Jesus was no rebel bandit, whatever Rome's charge would say.

settings.what: The hearing before the high priest and the council
settings.by: the high priest, the chief priests and the Sanhedrin; Jesus
settings.to: Jesus, and false witnesses
settings.when: that night, in the high priest's house. Luke 22:66–71 sets the council's questioning at daybreak, not at night
settings.why: for the council, to find a charge that could bring a death sentence; for Jesus, to answer the one question that mattered, whether he is the Messiah, and to warn his judges that they will see him vindicated
settings.readers: Christians who stood before councils (13:9) saw their Lord tried first, and heard his open confession. Mark's account has often been read as "the Jews condemned Jesus"; Mark names a ruling group meeting at night, not a people.
views: Mark presents a capital trial that broke the rules later written in the Mishnah.
Many historians think it was an inquiry by the high priest's circle to prepare a charge for Pilate (Brown, Sanders).

settings.to: a slave girl of the high priest and the bystanders in the courtyard
settings.when: at the same time as Jesus' hearing, before the rooster's second crow. Luke 22:54–62 tells all three denials before the hearing, and John 18:15–27 splits them around it
settings.why: to save himself by denying that he knew Jesus
settings.readers: If Mark's readers had been tested, as Pliny later tested Christians, by being told to curse Christ, Peter's failure and tears spoke to anyone who had denied under pressure, and the message "and Peter" (16:7) spoke of forgiveness.

title: The King on a Cross
sum: At first light the council hands Jesus over to Pilate. Pilate asks, "So you are the King of the Jews?" and is amazed at Jesus' silence. Offered the choice, the crowd stirred up by the chief priests asks for Barabbas, a rebel, and shouts "Crucify him!" Pilate, wanting to keep them happy, frees Barabbas and has Jesus whipped and crucified.

Soldiers dress Jesus in purple, crown him with thorns and salute him as king. Simon of Cyrene is forced to carry the cross to Golgotha. At the third hour they crucify him between two bandits under the notice "The King of the Jews," while passers-by, chief priests and the bandits mock him. From noon darkness covers the land. At the ninth hour Jesus cries out in Aramaic the opening of Psalm 22, "My God, my God, why have you abandoned me?" and dies with a loud cry. The sanctuary curtain is torn in two, and the centurion says, "This man really was God's Son!"

Women who had followed him from Galilee watch from a distance. Joseph of Arimathea, a respected council member, boldly asks Pilate for the body, wraps it in linen and lays it in a rock-cut tomb before the Sabbath begins. Two of the women see where he is laid.
readings: Read as history

Jesus' crucifixion under Pontius Pilate is one of the surest facts of ancient history, attested by Tacitus and Josephus as well as by the Gospels. Crucifixion was Rome's punishment for slaves and rebels; the charge "King of the Jews" fits a death for sedition. Historians debate the Barabbas custom, the role of the crowd, and how Pilate, known from other sources as harsh, came to look so hesitant.
Read as Mark's story

Mark tells the death of a king. The title "King of the Jews" is spoken by Pilate, saluted by soldiers, nailed above the cross, and twisted by the priests into "King of Israel." Every insult tells the truth without meaning to. At the end the heavens-torn-open of the baptism (1:10) is answered by the curtain torn in two, and the voice that said "You are my Son" is answered by a Gentile soldier.
Read with the Psalms

The chapter is soaked in Psalm 22 and Psalm 69: clothes divided by lots, heads shaking, sour wine to drink, and the cry "My God, my God." Mark seldom says "this fulfilled Scripture"; he tells the story in the words of the righteous sufferer, and readers who knew the psalms knew how they end: in God's rescue and in praise among the nations.

views.H: Pilate was prefect of Judea from AD 26 to 36; Philo and Josephus describe him as stubborn and harsh. Romans crucified rebels, bandits and slaves outside cities, often leaving bodies as a warning; in Judea they seem to have let Jews bury the crucified before nightfall (Josephus). The bones of a crucified man named Yehohanan, found in Jerusalem in 1968 with a nail still through the heel bone, show that a crucified Jew could receive burial in a family tomb. Golgotha lay just outside the city wall of the time; the Church of the Holy Sepulchre marks the traditional site.
views.C: Mark is probably the earliest account. Matthew adds Pilate's wife, the hand-washing and "His blood on us"; Luke adds the hearing before Herod, the women of Jerusalem, the penitent bandit and "Father, into your hands"; John has Jesus carry his own cross and say "It is finished." Mark's only word from the cross is the cry of Psalm 22. Many scholars think that the early church first told the passion as one connected story, which Mark used; others think Mark himself shaped it from separate memories and the psalms.
views.L: Mark marks the day in three-hour steps (15:1, 25, 33, 34, 42). The kingship theme runs through the chapter, and the mockery is full of irony: "Others he saved. Himself he cannot save." The torn curtain (15:38) and the centurion's confession (15:39) form the climax of the Gospel's opening line, which calls Jesus the Son of God (1:1). On three men named Simon around the passion, see Claude's theory on this page.
views.J: The crowd in Mark is a group gathered at the governor's court and stirred up by the chief priests, not the Jewish people; Mark has no line like Matthew 27:25. Jesus dies with a Jewish prayer on his lips, in Aramaic. A Jewish council member gives him burial according to the Law (Deuteronomy 21:23). Jewish and Christian historians alike have shown how later readings of this chapter fed the charge of "deicide" against Jews, a charge the Catholic Church rejected in 1965 (Nostra Aetate 4) and many other churches have rejected since.
views.T: The church has read this chapter on Good Friday from the earliest times, and the Stations of the Cross follow its scenes. The fathers saw Christ's kingship revealed in the cross and the torn curtain as the end of the old sanctuary and the opening of the way to God. The cry "My God, my God" was read by Athanasius and others as Christ speaking for humanity, and by the Reformers as Christ bearing the abandonment due to sinners. The centurion became, in later legend, a saint named Longinus.

deep.h: The hours of the crucifixion: Mark and John
deep.b:
Mark gives a clock: at first light the council hands Jesus to Pilate (15:1); "it was the third hour, and they crucified him" (15:25), about 9 a.m.; darkness from the sixth hour to the ninth (15:33), noon to 3 p.m.; at the ninth hour the cry and death (15:34–37); and then evening (15:42). John 19:14 says that Pilate brought Jesus out for the last time "about the sixth hour," about noon, before the crucifixion. Matthew and Luke keep Mark's sixth and ninth hours but drop the third.

  • A copying error. Greek numerals for 3 (Γ) and 6 (Ϛ) could be confused; some early writers suggested that one Gospel's number was miscopied. No manuscript evidence settles it.
  • Different reckoning. Some (following B. F. Westcott) argued that John counts hours from midnight, as Roman legal time did, so his "sixth hour" is 6 a.m. Most scholars doubt that John uses that system.
  • Rough times. Without clocks, people named the time by the nearest quarter of the day: the third hour could cover the whole mid-morning, the sixth the late morning to noon.
  • Theological times. John's hour matches the time the Passover lambs began to be slaughtered; Mark's three-hour steps match the Roman watches and the Jewish hours of prayer. The writers may care more about meaning than about the minute.

deep.h: God's Son, from the torn heavens to the torn curtain
deep.b:
Mark's opening line announces the good news of Jesus Christ, the Son of God (1:1; some early manuscripts lack the last words). Only twice does a voice from heaven speak: at the baptism, when the heavens are "torn open" and the Spirit comes down (1:10–11), and at the transfiguration (9:7). Demons know who he is (3:11; 5:7), but Jesus silences them. The high priest asks whether he is "the Son of the Blessed One," and Jesus says "I am" (14:61–62).

At his death Mark uses the Greek verb σχίζω ("tear") for the second and last time: the sanctuary curtain is torn in two (15:38). Other tearing in the story uses other Greek verbs, and the Plain gives them other English: "tear down" the sanctuary (καταλύω, 14:58; 15:29) and the high priest "ripped" his clothes (διαρρήγνυμι, 14:63). Josephus says the great curtain at the entrance of the sanctuary was woven with a picture of the heavens, so a first-century reader who knew the Temple might have seen the heavens torn again. Then for the first time in the Gospel a human being calls Jesus God's Son, and it is a Roman officer, at the moment of his most shameful death. Whatever the soldier meant by it (see the note at 15:39), Mark has placed it as the answer to his whole book: Jesus is known as God's Son not by miracles, and not by coming down from the cross, but by the way he dies.

Matthew 27 has the deep dives on "His blood on us, and on our children" (Matthew 27:25), its meaning and its misuse, and on who was responsible for Jesus' death. Mark's account differs in ways that matter for that question: it has no curse from the crowd, it blames "the chief priests" by name for stirring up the crowd (15:11) and for jealousy (15:10), and it shows Pilate choosing to please a crowd rather than to do justice (15:15). Mark's readers, living under Rome, were also reminded that it was Roman soldiers who mocked, whipped and crucified their Lord. The New Testament's own summary is that many hands were involved, and that all of them, Jew and Gentile, belonged to a world that needed the death they caused (Acts 4:27–28).

deep.title: Claude's theory: three Simons
deep.b: Mark names three men called Simon around the passion. Simon the man with skin disease hosts the meal at which Jesus is anointed for burial (14:3). Simon Peter, whom Jesus calls "Simon" in Gethsemane (14:37), had heard that anyone who would follow him must "pick up his cross" (8:34), and he denies Jesus. Simon of Cyrene, a stranger coming in from the country, is forced to pick up Jesus' cross and carry it (15:21). I suggest that Mark lets the repeated name make a point: the Simon who was called fails to carry the cross, and a Simon who was never called carries it, while a third, an outcast by his disease, opens his house. That the Cyrenian does what Peter was called to do is often noticed; the threefold pattern, and the meaning I give it, are my own reading and may be a coincidence of a very common name.

echoes: Psalm 22:1; Psalm 22:7; Psalm 22:18; Psalm 69:21; Isaiah 50:6; Isaiah 53:7; Isaiah 53:12; Amos 8:9; Deuteronomy 21:22–23; Exodus 26:31–33; Matthew 27:1–61; Luke 23:1–56; John 18:28–19:42; Romans 16:13; Hebrews 10:19–20

settings.to: Jesus
settings.when: early in the morning, at the governor's court in Jerusalem
settings.why: for Pilate, to learn whether this man claimed to be a king and was a danger to Rome; for the chief priests, to make the charges stick
settings.readers: For Christians who might stand before Roman governors (13:9), Jesus' near-silence and his short answer showed how to face a hostile court.

settings.to: the crowd that had come up to ask for the customary release, stirred by the chief priests
settings.when: at the Passover festival
settings.why: Pilate, knowing the priests acted from jealousy, tried to free Jesus by the custom, but in the end chose to keep the crowd satisfied
settings.readers: Mark's readers saw a Roman judge give in to pressure, and an innocent man condemned in place of a guilty one, a picture many have read as a sign of Jesus dying in place of others.
views: Some historians accept a local Passover release not recorded elsewhere.
Others think the custom is doubtful and the scene was shaped by early Christian reflection on Jesus' innocence.

settings.by: the Roman auxiliary soldiers in the Praetorium
settings.to: Jesus
settings.when: after the flogging, before the crucifixion
settings.why: to mock a so-called Jewish king with a game of salute and homage, with the cruelty soldiers showed condemned men
settings.readers: Readers who honored Jesus as King and bowed before him in worship saw the irony: the soldiers' mockery told the truth.

settings.by: passers-by, the chief priests with the scribes, and the two men crucified with him
settings.to: Jesus, and to one another
settings.when: while he hung on the cross, from the third hour
settings.why: to shame him: if he were the Messiah, he would come down and save himself
settings.readers: Mark's readers knew the answer: he did not save himself so that he could save others (8:35; 10:45), and they were called to the same way.

settings.to: God ("My God")
settings.when: at the ninth hour, after three hours of darkness, just before his death
settings.why: to pray the first line of Psalm 22, the lament of a righteous sufferer abandoned by God and mocked by enemies
settings.readers: Mark's readers, many of whom knew the psalm, heard both the depth of Jesus' abandonment and the psalm's turn toward God's rescue and praise.
views: Jesus truly experienced God-forsakenness, bearing sin or judgment for others.
By praying Psalm 22, Jesus claims its whole movement, from lament to vindication.

settings.by: the Roman centurion in charge of the execution
settings.to: those standing near, as he watched Jesus die
settings.when: immediately after Jesus' death
settings.why: to say what he saw in the way Jesus died: that this man really was God's Son
settings.readers: For Gentile Christians in Rome or elsewhere, the first human confession of Jesus as God's Son in Mark came from one of their own: a Roman soldier.

title: He Is Going Ahead of You
sum: When the Sabbath is over, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome buy spices to anoint Jesus' body. At sunrise on Sunday they come to the tomb, wondering who will roll away the stone, and find it rolled back. Inside, a young man in white tells them: "He has been raised. He isn't here." They are to tell his disciples, and Peter, that he is going ahead of them to Galilee. The women flee, shaking, and say nothing to anyone, "for they were afraid." In the oldest manuscripts the Gospel ends there.

Most manuscripts continue with the Longer Ending (16:9–20), translated here under its own heading: the risen Jesus appears to Mary Magdalene, then to two disciples in the country, then to the Eleven, whom he rebukes for unbelief and sends to proclaim the good news to every creature, promising signs to those who believe. He is taken up into heaven, and they go out and preach everywhere. A few manuscripts have a Shorter Ending instead or as well, and one adds a further saying after 16:14 (see the variants).

This page sets out the evidence for how Mark ends, the debate over whether Mark meant to stop at 16:8, and how the later endings draw on the other Gospels and Acts, with Where Christians differ cards on baptism (16:16), the signs (16:17–18), and the status of the Longer Ending as Scripture.
readings: Read as Mark wrote it (ending at 16:8)

The story stops with a promise and with silence. Jesus has been raised and is going ahead to Galilee, as he said (14:28), but no appearance is told and the women run away afraid. Many scholars think this was Mark's design: the reader knows the promise and must decide whether to follow, to tell, to go to Galilee. The good news has a "beginning" (1:1) and no ending, because the readers are meant to carry it on.
Read as the church's Bible (with 16:9–20)

For most of Christian history, in the Greek East and the Latin West, Mark was read with the Longer Ending, which gathers the appearances, the commission, the signs and the ascension into a short summary. It has been read in the liturgy on Easter and Ascension, and it has shaped preaching on mission, baptism and healing. Read this way, Mark ends like the other Gospels, with the risen Lord sending his followers to the world.
Read as history

The empty tomb and the women as its first witnesses are in all four Gospels; the earliest written list of appearances is Paul's (1 Corinthians 15:3–8, written in the 50s). Historians who accept the resurrection point to the empty tomb, the appearances and the sudden faith of the disciples; skeptical historians explain the stories as visions or later legend. Mark's account is the oldest narrative of the empty tomb.

views.H: Jewish tombs were visited in the days after burial, and anointing the dead was a loving duty. A tomb closed with a large stone, a young man in white, and three named women fit the setting of a Jerusalem burial. The Longer Ending reflects the life of the church in the late first and early second centuries: preaching "everywhere," baptism, exorcism, tongues and healing, all known from Acts and Paul's letters.
views.C: Almost all scholars agree that 16:9–20 was not written by the author of 1:1–16:8, on the evidence of the manuscripts, the early fathers, its vocabulary, style and content (see the deep dives). Whether Mark meant to end at 16:8 or his ending was lost is still debated. Matthew and Luke, who used Mark, both go on from the empty tomb to appearances, but in different directions, which some take as a sign that their copies of Mark ended at 16:8.
views.L: Mark's ending answers his beginning and his middle. The young man in white (16:5) recalls the young man who fled (14:51); the women's alarm repeats Jesus' own in Gethsemane (14:33); "he is going ahead of you" fulfills 14:28; "and Peter" answers the denial. After a Gospel full of people told to keep silent who spoke, the women are told to speak and keep silent. The abrupt ending forces readers to supply the rest from what Jesus has promised.
views.J: Belief in the resurrection of the dead was common among first-century Jews, Pharisees above all (Daniel 12:2; 2 Maccabees 7), but as a general event at the end of the age. The claim that God had raised one man ahead of the rest was new. Jewish writers such as Pinchas Lapide have taken the resurrection accounts seriously as Jewish testimony; others, then and now, explained the empty tomb otherwise (compare Matthew 28:11–15).
views.T: The Longer Ending has been part of the church's Bible since at least the late second century: Irenaeus quotes 16:19 as Mark's, and Tatian's Diatessaron includes it. Its verses on baptism (16:16) and signs (16:17–18) entered the church's teaching on the sacraments and on healing, and 16:19 shaped the creeds' confession that Christ "ascended into heaven and is seated at the right hand of the Father." In art, Mark's symbol, the lion, was often linked with the resurrection, the lion that rises.

deep.b:
Manuscripts that end at 16:8. The two oldest manuscripts that contain the end of Mark, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (both 300s), end the Gospel at 16:8 and add only the title. In Vaticanus the scribe left the rest of the column and the whole next column blank, the only such gap in its New Testament; some think he knew of another ending and left room for it. In Sinaiticus the leaf that holds the end of Mark is a replacement written by one of the original correctors, with the writing spread out. The Sinaitic Syriac (about 400), about a hundred Armenian manuscripts, and the two oldest Georgian manuscripts also end at 16:8.

The early writers. Clement of Alexandria and Origen, who quote Mark, never quote 16:9–20. Eusebius of Caesarea, early in the 300s, wrote that the accurate copies end at "for they were afraid" and that the longer ending is found in only some. Jerome, about 406, said that almost all Greek copies lacked it, yet he kept it in the Latin Vulgate; his letter largely repeats Eusebius' answer, so it is not independent evidence. Later Greek writers repeat the observation.

Manuscripts with the Longer Ending (16:9–20). Most Greek manuscripts from the 400s on (Alexandrinus, Ephraemi, Bezae (whose Greek has 16:9–15, the rest supplied much later), Washington and the great majority of later copies), the Latin Vulgate, most Syriac and Coptic versions. Irenaeus quotes 16:19 about AD 180 as from the end of Mark, and Tatian used it in his Diatessaron about 170, so the Longer Ending existed by the middle of the second century. Justin Martyr, about 155, may echo 16:20. Some manuscripts mark it with notes or symbols saying that older copies lack it.

The Shorter Ending. Two sentences saying that the women reported briefly to "those around Peter" and that Jesus sent out through them "the holy and undying message of eternal salvation." It stands alone in one Old Latin manuscript, Codex Bobiensis (k, about 400), and before the Longer Ending in several Greek manuscripts from the 600s on (083, 099, 0112, L, Ψ, 579) and some versions. See the variant at 16:8.

The Freer Logion. Codex Washington (W, 400s) adds after 16:14 an exchange in which the disciples blame Satan for their unbelief and Jesus answers that Satan's years are fulfilled. Jerome knew part of it. See the variant at 16:14.

The style. The Longer Ending uses many words found nowhere else in Mark, lacks Mark's favorite "immediately" and "again," begins with a new subject and reintroduces Mary Magdalene as if 16:1–8 had not been told, and summarizes appearances known from Luke, John and Acts. Most scholars, including those who defend its place in the canon, conclude that a later writer composed it. A few, such as Maurice Robinson, argue that it is original and that the shorter manuscripts are a local Egyptian tradition. The views are set out side by side in Perspectives on the Ending of Mark: Four Views (2008).

deep.h: Did Mark mean to stop at 16:8?
deep.b:
• Yes, on purpose. R. H. Lightfoot (1950), Frank Kermode (1979), J. Lee Magness (1986) and many scholars since argue that the abrupt ending fits Mark's art. The promise of 16:7 has been made and repeated (14:28); Mark's readers know the disciples did see Jesus, because the church exists. Ending on the women's fear leaves readers facing the same choice: to fear and fall silent, or to go to Galilee and tell. Ancient books could end on γάρ, "for" (Pieter van der Horst, 1972).
  • No, the ending was lost. N. Clayton Croy (2003) and others argue that Mark's last page was torn off or damaged, perhaps along with the first (Mark 1:1 also begins abruptly). A Gospel that announces appearances in Galilee (14:28; 16:7) would be expected to tell one, as Matthew does (Matthew 28:16–20). R. T. France and N. T. Wright have found this view likely.
  • No, Mark never finished. Some suggest Mark was prevented, by death, arrest or flight, from writing the last section.

All agree that someone in the second century, finding the ending too abrupt or missing, supplied one; in fact several did.

deep.h: The Longer Ending and the other Gospels
deep.b:
Almost every element of 16:9–20 has a parallel elsewhere in the New Testament, which is why many scholars think its writer drew on them:

  • First appearance to Mary Magdalene, out of whom seven demons had gone (16:9): John 20:11–18; Luke 8:2.
  • She tells mourning disciples, who disbelieve (16:10–11): John 20:18; Luke 24:10–11.
  • Two walking in the country, Jesus "in a different form" (16:12–13): Luke 24:13–35.
  • Appearance to the Eleven at table and rebuke of unbelief (16:14): Luke 24:36–43; John 20:19–29.
  • Commission to all the world (16:15): Matthew 28:19; Luke 24:47; Acts 1:8.
  • Believe and be baptized (16:16): Acts 2:38; Acts 16:31–33.
  • Demons, tongues, snakes, healing (16:17–18): Acts 2:4; 16:18; 28:3–8; Luke 10:17–19.
  • Taken up and seated at God's right hand (16:19): Luke 24:51; Acts 1:9–11; Psalm 110:1.
  • Preaching everywhere, with confirming signs (16:20): Acts 14:3; Hebrews 2:3–4.

James Kelhoffer (2000) argues that the writer knew all four Gospels and composed the ending in the early second century to give Mark a fitting close and to show that God confirmed the apostles' message by signs.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the beginning that does not end
deep.b: Mark's first words are "The beginning of the good news" (1:1), and his last, in the oldest manuscripts, are the women's silent flight (16:8). I suggest that Mark meant the whole book as only the beginning: the story of Jesus up to the empty tomb is the start of a good news that continues wherever the disciples, regathered in Galilee as promised (14:28; 16:7), take it to "all the nations" (13:10; 14:9). On this reading the missing appearances are not lost but deliberately left to the reader's own life and to the church's preaching, and 13:10 and 14:9 are Mark's way of telling the reader that the story does go on. This overlaps closely with readings by Morna Hooker, J. Lee Magness and others who connect 1:1 with 16:8; my contribution is only to tie it to the two "good news to the world" sayings, and it cannot be proved.

echoes: Psalm 110:1; 2 Kings 2:11; Daniel 12:2; Matthew 28:1–20; Luke 24:1–53; John 20:1–29; Acts 1:1–11; Acts 2:38; Acts 28:3–6; 1 Corinthians 15:3–8; Hebrews 2:3–4

settings.what: The young man's message at the tomb
settings.by: a young man in a white robe, sitting in the tomb
settings.to: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome
settings.when: at sunrise on the first day of the week, inside the empty tomb
settings.why: to calm their alarm, to announce that the crucified Jesus has been raised, and to send them to tell the disciples, and Peter in particular, that Jesus is going ahead of them to Galilee as he promised
settings.readers: Mark's readers, who knew the risen Lord in their own faith, heard the message as also sent to them, and the special mention of Peter as the promise of forgiveness to one who had failed.

settings.by: an unknown Christian writer, not the author of 16:1–8 on most scholars' view
settings.to: churches that read Mark, probably in the early second century
settings.when: some decades after Mark wrote; it was known by about AD 170–180
settings.why: to give Mark's Gospel an ending with appearances of the risen Jesus, a commission to the world, promised signs and the ascension, drawing on the other Gospels and Acts, and to stress that unbelief is rebuked and faith confirmed
settings.readers: Readers of Mark from the late second century on, who received it as the end of the Gospel; today's readers, who see it set apart in their Bibles.
views: It was first written as a summary of the resurrection appearances and later attached to Mark (Kelhoffer and many others).
It was composed to complete Mark, whose ending seemed too abrupt or was lost.
A minority holds that Mark wrote it and that the manuscripts lacking it are a local tradition (Robinson).

settings.by: the risen Jesus, as the Longer Ending tells it
settings.to: the Eleven, at a meal
settings.when: after he rebuked their unbelief
settings.why: to send them to proclaim the good news to every creature, to set before every hearer the choice between belief and unbelief, and to promise signs that would go along with believers
settings.readers: For second-century churches, the commission and signs confirmed that their mission, baptism, exorcisms and healings came from the risen Lord himself.

traditions.q: "The one who has believed and been baptized will be saved" (16:16). Is baptism necessary for salvation?
views: Baptism is necessary for salvation for those to whom the Gospel has been proclaimed and who have had the possibility of asking for it; the Church knows no other means of assuring entry into eternal life (Catechism 1257, citing this verse). God is not bound by his sacraments: those who die for the faith, or who desire baptism but die before receiving it, are saved (baptism of blood and of desire, Catechism 1258–1260).

Baptism is the new birth by water and the Spirit, through which a person is joined to Christ's death and resurrection and enters the Church; it is the normal and necessary door to salvation, though God's mercy is not limited by it.

Baptism "works forgiveness of sins, delivers from death and the devil, and gives eternal salvation to all who believe," as the Small Catechism says, quoting this verse; the Augsburg Confession calls it necessary for salvation. Yet it is unbelief, not lack of baptism, that condemns, as the second half of the verse shows.

Baptism is a sign and seal of the covenant of grace that must not be neglected, but "grace and salvation are not so inseparably annexed unto it, as that no person can be regenerated or saved without it" (Westminster Confession 28.5).

Baptism is the immersion of a believer, an act of obedience that pictures faith in Christ's death and resurrection; it does not save. Salvation is by grace through faith, and the verse condemns only the one who does not believe (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article 7).

Churches of Christ teach that the Lord's order is believe, be baptized, be saved: immersion of a penitent believer is for the forgiveness of sins (Acts 2:38), and this verse is one of the plainest statements of it.

traditions.q: "Signs like these will follow those who have believed" (16:17–18): tongues, healing, safety from snakes and poison. Do these signs continue in the church today?
views: Yes. The baptism in the Holy Spirit is shown by speaking in other tongues, and divine healing is provided for in Christ's atonement (Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths). The large Pentecostal bodies do not handle snakes or drink poison: they read 16:18 as God's protection in danger that comes unsought, as with Paul on Malta (Acts 28:3–6).

The Holy Spirit still gives charisms, extraordinary or simple, for building up the Church, including healing and tongues; they are to be received with gratitude and discerned by the Church's pastors (Catechism 799–801). The Catholic Charismatic Renewal is an approved movement within the Church.

Miracles continue in the life of the Church, especially through the prayers of the saints, holy relics and the sacrament of holy unction, but the Church does not seek signs for their own sake or treat any one gift as the proof of the Spirit.

Many Reformed theologians are cessationists: the miraculous signs were given to confirm the apostles and their message (Hebrews 2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 12:12) and ceased when that foundation was laid (B. B. Warfield, Counterfeit Miracles, 1918). Warfield did not build on 16:17–20, which he held Mark did not write. Others in the Reformed world, such as some charismatic Calvinists, hold that the gifts continue.

traditions.q: Most scholars think Mark did not write 16:9–20. Is it Scripture all the same?
views: Yes. The Council of Trent received the books of Scripture "entire with all their parts, as they have been accustomed to be read in the Catholic Church, and as they are contained in the old Latin Vulgate," which includes these verses. Catholic Bibles print them as canonical. In 1912 the Pontifical Biblical Commission ruled that the arguments did not prove Mark had not written them; since the 1950s, when the Commission's officers said its earlier rulings on such questions no longer bound scholars, Catholic scholars have been free to hold that someone other than Mark wrote them.
Yes. The Longer Ending has always been read in the Orthodox Church: it is one of the eleven resurrection Gospels read in turn at Sunday Matins, and it is received as Scripture without question.

Divided. The Thirty-Nine Articles receive the canonical books without listing verses. In the nineteenth century Anglican scholars led both sides of the debate: John Burgon defended the verses as Mark's own (1871), while B. F. Westcott and F. J. A. Hort judged them an early addition and printed them apart (1881).

Divided. Most evangelical scholars and modern translations judge that Mark did not write 16:9–20 and print it with a note, and many will not base a doctrine on it alone; others, including defenders of the Byzantine or Received Text such as Maurice Robinson, hold it to be original and fully Scripture. The range of views is set out in Perspectives on the Ending of Mark: Four Views (2008).
